title: Knowledge Check 2: Lessons 6-10
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 6-10 of the hermes-consultant series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson “When an Agent Is the Right Tool, and When to Say No”, what is the central focus?
options: The honest consultant's rule: an agent is not always the right answer, and the consultant who can say no protects both the client's money and their own reputation.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The honest consultant's rule: an agent is not always the right answer, and the consultant who can say no protects both the client's money and their own reputation. How to tell the work an agent should do from the work it should never touch, and how to walk away cleanly.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
Lesson 5 taught you how to map every stakeholder who can stop an implementation.
The opposite is true: lesson 5 taught you how to map every stakeholder who can stop an implementation.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
questions.explanation: Lesson 5 taught you how to map every stakeholder who can stop an implementation.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
Here is a practical filter you can run against any request before you commit.
Here is not a practical filter you can run against any request before you commit.
questions.explanation: Here is a practical filter you can run against any request before you commit.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Installing and Deploying Hermes Agent: Local Setup, Profiles, Gateway, First Run”, what is the central focus?
options: The consultant's deployment discipline: how to stand up an agent correctly once you have the go-ahead. Isolation per engagement, a verified first run before you layer on features, and a gateway that turns a laptop experiment into an always-on tool your client actually uses.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The consultant's deployment discipline: how to stand up an agent correctly once you have the go-ahead. Isolation per engagement, a verified first run before you layer on features, and a gateway that turns a laptop experiment into an always-on tool your client actually uses.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
Lesson 6 taught you when an agent is not the right tool and when to say no.
Lesson 6 taught you when an agent is the right tool and when to say no.
questions.explanation: Lesson 6 taught you when an agent is the right tool and when to say no.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: On native Windows it is not the PowerShell equivalent.
On native Windows it is the PowerShell equivalent.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.
questions.explanation: On native Windows it is the PowerShell equivalent.

questions.question: Per the lesson about configuration, what is the central focus?
options: A list of available reasoning models
The model, provider, and fallback choices that make an agent dependable are part of the deliverable, not an install detail
A review of unrelated database tools
A summary of marketing policy
questions.explanation: The lesson treats configuration as a contract with the client's future, covering model and provider separation, secrets, verification, and fallbacks.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Model and provider are the same thing and belong together in one setting
Secrets and settings belong in the same file so the config is easier to copy
Keep the model and the provider as separate keys so you can swap each independently
Verify a setting only by re-reading the config file you edited
questions.explanation: The lesson argues you must be able to swap the provider while keeping the model and vice versa, which requires keeping them as separate keys.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The config file is always the value that runs, so precedence does not matter
Fallbacks only trigger on complete provider shutdowns and never cost anything
An agent with no fallback is fine because providers rarely fail
If you never verify what the running agent resolved, it works on my machine can be true for a reason you do not understand
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that precedence layers can override your file, so you must verify what actually runs, and an agent without a fallback is not dependable.

questions.question: Per the lesson about tools and skills, what is the central focus?
options: A history of agent frameworks
What an agent can do comes from its tools, how it does it well comes from its skills, and how to know what is real in the running system
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of network policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the capability discipline of telling real capabilities from claimed ones and extending an agent without writing code.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A tool tells the agent how to act the client's way, and a skill lets it act
The registry is a guarantee that all tools are available in every session
A missing skill means the agent physically cannot do the task
Availability varies by platform, credentials, and which toolsets are enabled, so treat the registry as a claim and the running agent as the evidence
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that ships with is not a guarantee of availability, so you answer capability questions from observed behavior.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: An installed skill is always current because it was written recently
A skill is a substitute for a capability the agent lacks
A capability is real only when you have evidence it fired, a tool call, an artifact, or returned output, not the agent's word
Trust the agent's report of its own work because it knows what it did
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a capability is real only when you have watched it fire, and skills rot so they must be verified against the live system.

questions.question: Per the lesson about MCP servers and integrations, what is the central focus?
options: Wiring an agent into the client's stack through MCP, deciding what it gets to touch, and proving the connection in the running system
A history of API standards
A review of unrelated database tools
A summary of network policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the three disciplines of integration: naming what an integration is, deciding the boundary, and proving the connection.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Give the agent every action the integration server offers so it is flexible
The transport is the interesting decision because stdio is safer than HTTP
Expose only the narrow set of actions the scoped task requires and deliberately withhold the dangerous ones
Install a one-click catalog server without reading what it runs
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches least privilege: give the agent the narrowest set of actions that lets it do the job, and remove the dangerous actions from reach entirely.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Configuring a server is the same as connecting to it
The integration is only real when you have watched it fire against the live system on a real task
Hand your whole shell environment to the MCP subprocess so it has what it needs
A failed MCP tool call may safely echo a credential into the conversation
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the verification reflex: you do not trust the connection because you configured it; you give the agent a real task and watch it work end to end.
